Contact 2 asks the recipient to read aloud a verification code that was sent to confirm the recipient's own identity, a request no legitimate support contact makes, by design of the item.

items.answer: A verification code sent to your phone exists to prove that only you, not the caller, can access your account; reading it to the caller hands them exactly the proof they need to get in, even if they sound official.

verification.reasoning: An acceptable answer must explain that the code's purpose is to prove the account holder's identity to the account holder alone, and that sharing it defeats that purpose.

Contact 3 requires no immediate response and directs any question to a phone number printed on the recipient's own card rather than one supplied by the sender, matching the unit's legitimate-contact pattern by design.

items.answer: In Contact 3, the learner would call a number printed on their own card, a number they control and trust; in Contacts 1 and 2, the sender supplies the link or expects the learner to respond directly to them, so the sender controls the contact point instead.

verification.reasoning: An acceptable answer must identify who controls the response channel (the recipient's own trusted source versus the sender) as the deciding safety feature.

items.answer: An acceptable three-step plan: (1) do not click any link, call back, or respond with any information; (2) independently look up or use an already-known, trusted phone number or contact method, not one supplied in the message; (3) tell a trusted adult about the message before taking any further action.
